sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Fiber appears in Go job postings and conference talks primarily because of its benchmark numbers, and candidates are expected to know what those benchmarks actually mean. Fiber is built on fasthttp rather than net/http, which gives it measurably lower allocation counts and higher throughput in synthetic benchmarks. However, this comes with a fundamental compatibility break from the stdlib and a sharp concurrency footgun that has caused real production bugs. Understanding Fiber's trade-offs — not just its upside — is what interviewers are looking for.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: fasthttp's performance comes from aggressively reusing request and response objects: instead of allocating a new `*http.Request` per connection, fasthttp maintains a pool and reuses the same struct, zeroing and repopulating it for each request. This eliminates millions of allocations per second under high load, which is the source of Fiber's benchmark advantage. The consequence is that `fiber.Ctx` is only valid for the lifetime of the handler function — once the handler returns, fasthttp recycles the Ctx and its underlying buffers. Reading a Ctx value in a goroutine that outlives the handler will return garbage or corrupted data.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **fasthttp foundation**: Fiber wraps github.com/valyala/fasthttp; the `fiber.Ctx` wraps fasthttp's RequestCtx, not net/http.
- **Fiber routing and ctx API**: `app.Get`, `app.Post`, route groups via `app.Group`; Express-inspired `c.Params`, `c.Query`, `c.BodyParser`, `c.JSON`, `c.Status`.
- **Fiber middleware**: `app.Use(func(c *fiber.Ctx) error { ... return c.Next() })` — similar model to Express.js.
- **Benchmark vs Gin comparison**: Fiber consistently wins on allocations-per-request and requests-per-second in synthetic benchmarks; the gap narrows significantly under real-world conditions with DB I/O.
- **stdlib incompatibility**: Fiber does NOT implement http.Handler; net/http middleware, httptest, and any library that accepts http.Handler cannot be used with Fiber directly.
- **c.Locals for goroutine-safe value passing**: use `c.Locals(key, value)` to attach values to the request context, but copy all data out before spawning goroutines.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Fiber ctx must not be stored across goroutine boundaries**: if you spawn `go func() { doSomething(c) }()`, the goroutine may access `c` after fasthttp has recycled it for a new request — read all values from `c` before the goroutine call, then pass copies.
- **stdlib middleware does NOT work with Fiber**: no httptest, no net/http middleware ecosystem — you must use Fiber-specific middleware or write adapters.
- **Most production services are not bottlenecked on HTTP framework overhead**: the bottleneck is almost always the database, external API calls, or business logic — not the framework's routing or request parsing.
- **When Fiber makes sense**: high-throughput proxy services, protocol gateways, or any service where profiling has confirmed the HTTP layer itself is the bottleneck.
- **fasthttp and HTTP/2**: fasthttp does not natively support HTTP/2; if you need HTTP/2, Fiber is not the right choice.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Fiber wins benchmarks but I only choose it when I've profiled and confirmed that HTTP framework overhead is actually the bottleneck — which is rare in services that talk to a database or external APIs. The performance comes from fasthttp reusing the request context object per connection, which means the fiber.Ctx is only valid inside the handler function and you cannot pass it to goroutines safely. The other trade-off I always call out is stdlib incompatibility: you lose httptest, the entire ecosystem of net/http middleware, and any library that accepts an http.Handler interface. For the vast majority of backend services, the performance difference versus Gin or Chi is unmeasurable in production, so I default to a stdlib-compatible framework and save Fiber for the rare case where I have data proving the framework itself is the bottleneck."
